title: Sublogarithmic competitiveness for online metric TSP
formal: Does there exist one deterministic online insertion algorithm \(A\), in the unrestricted-space model below, and a function \(\rho:\{2,3,\ldots\}\to[1,\infty)\) such that \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\rho(n)/\log_2 n=0\) and \(\operatorname{cost}_A(D)\le\rho(n)\operatorname{OPT}(D)\) for every \(n\ge2\) and every valid sequence of \(n\) metric arrivals? The algorithm knows \(n\), but receives distances only as points arrive and does not know the final offline optimum. Earlier relative-order decisions are irrevocable.
why: An online tour can insert new points between old ones while keeping the old relative order. The question asks how costly that one irreversible choice is when future distances are unknown. Its resolution would identify whether the logarithmic guarantee reflects an inherent online limitation or a limitation of known ordering rules.
status_note: Explicitly open in ICALP 2026 Section 4 and the checked 7 August 2026 full version. The capacity-dependent lower bounds do not settle the unrestricted insertion model. Bounded later checks through 2026-09-16 verified no resolution.

progress.text: The ESA paper specifies online ordering through the distances between consecutive array entries, with repeated points allowed. Its fixed-capacity results concern a stricter insertion model.

The ICALP paper improves the upper bound with a small amount of extra array capacity and proves a capacity-dependent deterministic lower bound. Section 4 explicitly leaves improving logarithmic competitiveness with unlimited space open.
The full arXiv version repeats the unlimited-space open question and the distinction between known and unknown offline optimum.

category_assignment.reason: The main target is the cost or competitive ratio of serving requests without knowledge of the future.

importance.reason: The question isolates the cost of irreversible online ordering in arbitrary metrics after computational and storage limits are removed. Breaking the longstanding logarithmic bound would separate this canonical geometric online problem from superficially similar irrevocable-edge problems and clarify how much adaptivity a growing tour retains.
importance.basis: Individual reading of ICALP 2026 Sections 1 and 4, its August full version, and the original online-ordering model in ESA 2024.

sentences: Points arrive with distances to earlier points and must immediately be inserted into an evolving order.
Each insertion preserves the relative order of all previous arrivals, but there is no fixed array capacity or computational resource bound.
The final cost is the sum of distances between consecutive points, compared with the best offline ordering.
The question asks whether a deterministic algorithm can guarantee a competitive ratio smaller than logarithmic by an asymptotic factor on every metric input.
This would isolate how much performance is lost through irreversible ordering alone, beyond the additional losses caused by limited storage.

definitions:
An instance of length \(n\) is a real symmetric matrix \(D=(d_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le n}\) with \(d_{ii}=0\), \(d_{ij}\ge0\), and \(d_{ij}\le d_{ik}+d_{kj}\) for all \(i,j,k\). Distinct arrival indices may have distance zero, representing repeated occurrences of the same point. Equivalently, this is a sequence of points in an arbitrary metric space, with repetitions permitted. There is no bound on the number of distinct points, metric dimension, nonzero distance ratios or magnitude of distances. Arrival indices carry no information beyond their order.

The integer \(n\) is given initially. At step \(t\), the algorithm receives exactly the vector \((d_{t1},\ldots,d_{t,t-1})\), in addition to the prefix information and its stored state. It must then choose a position for the new index \(t\) in its current ordered list. If \(\pi_{t-1}\) is the list before this step, \(\pi_t\) must be obtained by inserting \(t\) in one of its \(t\) gaps, including before its first and after its last element. The order of all earlier indices is preserved. The algorithm must finish this choice before receiving step \(t+1\). It has no access to distances involving future arrivals, a description of the ambient metric, future points, the final optimum, predictions or advice. There is no limit on the number of available insertion positions imposed by a fixed array, and no memory bound.

For a permutation \(\pi\) of \([n]\), define
\[
\ell_D(\pi)=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}d_{\pi(j),\pi(j+1)}.
\]
The final cost is \(\operatorname{cost}_A(D)=\ell_D(\pi_n)\), and \(\operatorname{OPT}(D)=\min_{\pi\in S_n}\ell_D(\pi)\), where \(S_n\) is the set of all permutations of \([n]\). Endpoints are free, and no return edge is charged; this follows the online-ordering source’s path-length convention. Costs at intermediate stages are not separately accumulated. There is no additive allowance in the competitive guarantee. When all arrivals coincide, \(\operatorname{OPT}=0\) and the multiplicative inequality still applies.

For explicit uniformity, an algorithm is a single finite deterministic program with ordinary binary integer control and exact real registers. It may copy real values, use \(0,1\), addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero value, and order or equality comparisons; its integer control may perform arbitrary finite bit computation. The revealed distances are exact real input values, rather than numerical approximations. Arbitrary real constants, advice indexed by \(n\), an oracle for unreceived distances and random instructions are unavailable. Each insertion decision must halt after finitely many operations on every valid prefix, but there is no running-time or storage bound. The quantity being compared is solely the length of the final ordering. This fixes an ideal exact-distance model; it does not impose polynomial-time optimization between arrivals.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of such a uniform deterministic algorithm and a sublogarithmic competitive bound for every valid input, or a complete Lean proof that no such algorithm exists. The proof must cover unrestricted metrics and all arrival orders, with a common \(\rho(n)=o(\log n)\). A constant-factor improvement to an \(O(\log n)\) bound, a lower bound for one particular insertion rule, or a lower bound requiring a restricted array capacity does not settle this target. No \(1/100\) additive tolerance is attached to this asymptotic resource comparison.

context_blocks.text: The selected sentence concerns improving the \(O(\log n)\) guarantee even with unlimited space. This card makes the deterministic branch in the surrounding paragraph explicit and interprets “improving” asymptotically as \(o(\log n)\). It does not require constant competitiveness or a near-linear array.

The model is online construction of an ordering. It is different from a traveling server that moves while new requests are released: here there are no release times, movement before the final ordering, deadlines or service constraints.

The ESA 2024 definition charges distances between consecutive occupied positions and allows repeated points. With arbitrary insertions and no fixed array capacity, only the relative order of previous arrivals is committed. Closing the path into a tour changes costs by at most a factor two in a metric, so that endpoint convention does not change the sublogarithmic existence question.

The 2026 source reports the classical \(O(\log n)\) guarantee for unrestricted insertion. Its new lower bound requires an array of limited size and therefore does not establish a logarithmic lower bound in the unrestricted-space model.

For \(m=(1+\varepsilon)n\), the 2026 paper gives a deterministic \(O(\log^3 n/\varepsilon)\) guarantee in its stated parameter range. This is progress on the space tradeoff, while the unlimited-space sublogarithmic question remains explicitly open in its closing remarks.

Model equivalence check: a final path has length no greater than its closure and the closure has length at most twice the path. Thus path/cycle competitive guarantees transfer with a constant factor, which preserves o(log n). The source’s finite-array restrictions are not carried into this card.
